, and as the Governor’s wife, Dorothy Quincy Hancock was obliged to entertain 300 naval officers during a visit from Admiral D’Estaing’s French fleet in 1778. Facing a shortage of milk, she improvised and sent servants to the Common to milk the community cows. If the Hancocks felt free to take from Boston Common, it was because they also added to it. Hancock provided a large cask of Madeira wine and a fireworks display for the celebration held on the Common in 1765 for the repeal of the Stamp Act, and built a bandstand on the Common in 1771. Boston Common has, and continues to, serve a higher purpose as a place for public oratory and discourse. Here, during the 20th century, Charles Lindbergh promoted commercial aviation; Anti-Vietnam War and civil rights rallies were held, including one led by Martin Luther King, Jr.; and in 1979 Pope John Paul II gave Mass to a gathered crowd. Today, Boston Common is open for all to enjoy. Robert Gould Shaw and 54th Regiment Memorial Dedicated in 1897, the bronze Robert Gould Shaw/54th Massachusetts Regiment Memorial, sculpted in bas-relief by Augustus Saint-Gaudens, commemorates the first all-Black volunteer regiment in the Civil War. Shaw and many of his men perished in their assault of Fort Wagner in South Carolina. William Carney, who was wounded in the assault, rescued the regiment’s battle flag and became the first black man to earn the Congressional Medal of Honor. You are here Home › Cemeteries › Granary Burying Ground Last updated: 2/20/26 Granary Burying Ground The Granary Burying Ground, located at 120 Tremont Street in downtown Boston, is the city's third oldest cemetery. The Granary Burying Ground was the third burial site in Boston Proper, established in 1660. Town officials set aside part of what was then the Boston Common for burial space to help alleviate overcrowding in the near-by King’s Chapel Burying Ground. First, the space was known as the South or Common Burying Ground, and then the Middle Burying Ground (after the opening of Central Burying Ground). The Granary Burying Ground took its present name in 1737 when a granary, a small building used to store grain, was moved to the site presently occupied by the Park Street Church. The Granary Burying Grounds contains approximately 2,345 gravestones and tombs, although it is estimated that over 5,000 people are buried at this site. The grave markers are predominantly slate. The gravestones’ original configuration was rearranged into straighter rows over the years to accommodate both nineteenth-century aesthetics and the modern lawnmower. Underground burial crypts (tombs) line the entire perimeter of the site. These crypts are small rectangular rooms, made of brick or stone, designed to hold multiple burials, which were frequently owned by families. sources.text: History – 263 Summer St Skip to content Skip to footer Apartments Studio Apartments One Bedroom Apartments Two Bedroom Apartments Amenities History The Neighborhood FAQs Contact Us Resident Portal History Close Apartments Studio Apartments One Bedroom Apartments Two Bedroom Apartments Amenities History The Neighborhood FAQs Contact Us Resident Portal facebook-1 twitter-x instagram Get in Touch! info@website.com Want to Work with Us? Send Brief Find Your Dream Apartment! Go to Shop The History of 263 Summer St A Building That Helped Shape the City Long before it became home, 263 Summer Street played a working role in Boston’s industrial rise. Constructed in 1905 by the Boston Wharf Company, the building was part of a network of warehouses, offices, and manufacturing spaces that defined Fort Point as one of the city’s most productive districts. Designed by architect Morton D. Safford , whose work helped shape the neighborhood, the building was created for durability, efficiency, and longevity—qualities that still define it today. From the start, this was a place built to last. Summer Street & “Wool Row” At the turn of the 20th century, Summer Street was known as “Wool Row” —the customer-facing edge of Boston’s wool and textile trade. Merchants, manufacturers, and logistics operations lined the corridor, connecting industry to the waterfront, the rail system, and the rest of the city. Early tenants reflected that energy and scale, including the U.S. Army Depot Quartermaster , Windrum Shoe Manufacturing , and the Boston Wool Trade Association . This building wasn’t ornamental—it was essential. Built on Resilience The story goes deeper than the brick walls. Fort Point itself was built on land created from the debris of Boston’s Great Fire of 1872 —a city-scale reset that led to a stronger, more modern Boston. That cycle of reinvention is literally beneath your feet, embedded in the character of the district, and carried forward by the buildings that rose from it. The Sign That Never Went Dark Rising above Summer Street is the iconic red neon “Boston Wharf Co Industrial Real Estate” sign—a fixture that has guided pedestrians and commuters for generations. Officially recognized within Fort Point’s landmark guidelines, the sign has been described as a beacon marking the passage from downtown into Boston’s industrial age. Over the years, it has been repainted and reinterpreted by local artists, reinforcing its role as more than signage—it’s a cultural marker. While much around it has changed, the sign remains, anchoring the building to its origins. A New Chapter Begins More than a century after its construction, 263 Summer Street enters its next era as part of Boston’s office-to-housing transformation—preserving what makes the building significant while reimagining what it can be. The exterior remains unmistakably historic. Inside, the spaces have been fully modernized for contemporary living, with clean lines, warm materials, and thoughtful layouts that respect the building’s industrial bones without replicating the past. This isn’t history frozen in time—it’s history, adapted. Still Standing. Still Evolving. Today, 263 Summer Street stands as a rare balance: a building with memory, character, and presence—redefined for the way Boston lives now. What began as a place of work has become a place to live. What was built for industry now supports community. And what has endured for more than a century continues to move forward. Contact Have a quest

sources.text: How to humanize a $22 billion neighborhood built from scratch | WS Development Who We Are What We Do Development Leasing Investment Capital Markets Construction Management Studio Brand Experience & Marketing Brand Partnerships Retail Incubation Insider Our Properties Retail Workplace News Careers Contact Who We Are What We Do Development Leasing Investment Capital Markets Construction Management Studio Brand Experience & Marketing Brand Partnerships Retail Incubation Insider Our Properties Retail Workplace News Careers Contact WS in the News October 6, 2021 – Fast Company Back How to humanize a $22 billion neighborhood built from scratch The heart of this massive Boston project is a rock-strewn park by James Corner Field Operations, the architects behind New York City’s High Line. The large-scale redevelopment of Boston’s Seaport district is part of a $22 billion dollar attempt to turn a working waterfront into a mixed-use urban neighborhood. Spread over 20 blocks on a former working harbor just outside of downtown, the district has long been slated to become an “innovation district,” with more than a dozen office towers, and space for residential and retail use. But making a neighborhood from scratch is not always easy. One of its key designers wanted to make sure it didn’t become an isolated dead zone. “The tendency for developments at this scale is the developer is always wanting to internalize the project, to turn it inwards,” says landscape architect James Corner, founder of James Corner Field Operations . “I always find those places bereft of urban life. They’re often empty and sterile simply because they’re not connected to anything.” It’s a common trait. Self-contained mega projects like New York’s Hudson Yards have been denounced for creating a sense of separation from their surroundings, and urban destinations like Baltimore’s Harborplace have been criticized for turning their backs on the neighborhoods that surround them. https://dyknfksv5ixrq.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Harbor-Way-Boston-Seaport_final.mp4 Instead, the master plan for the Seaport district, designed by architecture and urban design firm Sasaki , focused on forging connections to its impressive surroundings—the waterfront and the city’s downtown. Opening this month, the first completed phase of the project is Harbor Way, a linear promenade and central public park that carve pathways through the site. Corner, whose firm is known for its work on New York City’s High Line, calls it “a pedestrian armature” that will connect the city to the harbor. Situated in between blocks of complete and nearly complete buildings that will make up this mixed-use district when construction wraps in 2024, Harbor Way turns what could have been a street into a pedestrian-focused civic and commercial space. Lined with trees, seating areas, and the frontages of stores and restaurants, it’s intended to draw people in and also help redraw connections to the waterfront. The harbor itself became part of the inspiration for the design, Corner says. Weather-beaten wooden planks form a central boardwalk along the promenade, and the ropes, chains, steel, and iron of the shipping industry influenced the hardscape that cuts through the district. The linear promenade connects to a wider central green space that is intended to be used year-round, even through Boston’s generally frigid winters.
